backups.name: Walrus Glacier
backups.overview: Clark Mountain (8,602 ft) is the highest summit of the Dakobed Range, rising about 8 miles southeast of Glacier Peak at the head of the Boulder Creek/White River, Napeequa, and Chiwawa drainages within the Glacier Peak Wilderness. The mountain's south and west sides are open, rugged scree and heather slopes, while its glaciated north and east flanks carry the small Clark (Walrus) Glacier and the Richardson Glacier. Luahna Peak, about a mile northwest along the connecting ridge, is a common add-on for strong parties. Two standard lines are climbed: a non-glacier scree/Class 3 scramble up the south side, and the more scenic Walrus Glacier route approached from Boulder Pass, often called one of the most esthetic non-technical glacier climbs in the eastern Cascades.
backups.beta: Most parties camp at Boulder Basin and climb Clark as a two-day (sometimes three-day) trip. From camp, drop over Boulder Pass to a bench on Clark's eastern arm, gain the Walrus Glacier, and ascend a moderately steep chute on the glacier's left (south) margin, stepping over narrow crevasses and crossing at least one snow-bridge, to a short summit scramble. A glacier-free alternative (the 'Southeast Route') avoids the glacier via a gully out of the south basin but is not the line documented here.
backups.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround time before committing to the glacier chute — softening snow bridges over crevasses later in the day, deteriorating visibility/flat light (both reported as common on this glacier), and a rising afternoon flow at the unbridged Boulder Creek ford all argue for an early start and a conservative decision to retreat if conditions or weather sour.
backups.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at many trailheads.
backups.comms: No reliable cell coverage is reported in Boulder Basin or on Clark Mountain itself; the remoteness of the Glacier Peak Wilderness and the multi-day nature of the approach make a satellite communicator (e.g., inReach) advisable — Chelan County Sheriff's Office/SAR has responded to inReach-triggered rescues in this general area.
backups.descent: Reverse the Boulder Pass/Walrus Glacier line while the glacier is still firm, or come down the non-glacier south-side scree/Class 3 alternative; parties continuing on to Luahna Peak descend Clark's west side via a steep, loose ('choss'-filled) gully rather than returning the same way.
obj_haz: unbridged, multi-channel ford of Boulder Creek
loose rock on the summit scramble

waypoints.name: White River Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 6400 past Coles Corner/WA-207; $5 day-use fee or NW Forest Pass, self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk, vault toilet, no potable water.
waypoints.directions: From US-2 at Coles Corner take WA-207 about ten miles up past Lake Wenatchee, then White River Road / FS-6400 another ten miles to the road end. Pavement gives out partway along; the gravel that follows is rough but not rutted, and the trailhead has a large gravelled lot shared with the Indian Creek, Mount David and PCT approaches.

waypoints.name: Boulder Creek Trail #1562 junction
waypoints.note: White River Trail's first 4 miles are flat, brushy, and often overgrown; bear right (east) off White River Trail #1507 onto the unmaintained Boulder Creek Trail #1562.
waypoints.directions: Head south on White River Trail #1507 along the valley floor. Four miles of nearly flat walking with almost no gain, brushy in places and notoriously mosquito-heavy from early to mid summer. Bear right (east) at the junction onto Boulder Creek Trail #1562, which is unmaintained above this point.

waypoints.name: Boulder Creek ford
waypoints.note: Unbridged, knee-to-thigh-deep crossing at the top of Boulder Basin depending on snowmelt; swap to sandals, current is swift early season.
waypoints.directions: Boulder Creek Trail climbs steadily through forest for about four and a half miles into Boulder Creek Basin. The creek is unbridged and must be forded; early in the season it runs cold and knee- to thigh-deep and often braids into two or three separate channels, which is easier to read but wetter than a single crossing. Sandals are worth carrying for it.

waypoints.name: Boulder Basin camp
waypoints.note: Established backcountry camp used as the standard base for a Clark summit day; the unmaintained climbers' path to Boulder Pass/Walrus Glacier splits off climbers-left just past the campsites and can vanish into brush.
waypoints.directions: A short walk past the ford puts you in the open basin, where established camps are spread between roughly 4,900 and 5,300 ft — around 8.5 miles and 3,000 ft from the car. Water is reliable here and essentially absent above it, so this is where you fill for the summit day. Given the scale of the outing most parties base here rather than attempt it car-to-car.

waypoints.name: Boulder Pass
waypoints.note: Scenic saddle with airy views over both the White and Napeequa drainages; the non-glacier south-side scramble and the Walrus Glacier line to the summit diverge from here.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at camp and climb open heather and talus north toward the pass, picking up the climbers' path that breaks off climbers-left just past the campsites. It is a direct fall-line push and takes most parties around an hour and a half. Slopes in the basin below the pass hold wet-slide avalanche debris into early summer.

waypoints.name: Walrus (Clark) Glacier rope-up / crevasse zone
waypoints.note: Rope up here on the bench on Clark's eastern arm, across Boulder Pass, before stepping onto the ~0.3 sq mi Walrus Glacier; stay on the left (south) margin, several narrow crevasses and one large crevasse crossed on a snowbridge.
waypoints.directions: Go down steep snow on the far side of the pass, then climb to a bench around 6,700 ft on Clark's eastern arm and rope up there with crampons and axe. From the bench, traverse east across the basin beneath Peak 7242, crossing its northeast ridge at about that same height. Turn back west from there, roughly half an hour, to the toe of the glacier — it is labelled Clark Glacier on some maps. The non-glacier south-side line diverges back at the pass, so roping up here is the committing choice.

waypoints.name: Clark Mountain summit
waypoints.note: True summit of the Dakobed Range's high point, 8 mi southeast of Glacier Peak; final approach is a short scramble over summit rocks above the glacier or south-side scree.
waypoints.directions: Take the moderately steep chute on the glacier's left (south) margin, stepping over several narrow crevasses and crossing one larger one on a snow bridge whose condition changes through the season and through the day. Above the ice a short Class 3 scramble over the summit rocks, with a soft 45-50 degree snow traverse below the top, gains the true summit.

backups.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed; this is a glacier scramble rather than a roped rock climb. Bring a standard glacier-travel kit — ice axe, crampons, a rope for the team, and a basic crevasse-rescue rack (a few ice screws, prusik cords or mechanical ascenders, a pulley, and slings/carabiners) for the Walrus Glacier crossing, where narrow crevasses and at least one snow-bridge are typically encountered.
what_to_bring: trekking poles for Boulder Creek fords
pro_tips: Carry glacier gear for the Walrus/Clark Glacier crossing and rope up around 6,700-7,000 ft on its northeast side
Cross the glacier early in the day while snow bridges are firm
Camp at Boulder Basin or Boulder Pass to shorten summit day given the long approach
Ford Boulder Creek earlier in the day before afternoon snowmelt raises its flow
watch_out: hidden crevasses on the Walrus/Clark Glacier
loose rock and choss on the south ridge and the west gully used toward Luahna Peak
cold, swift, sometimes thigh-deep Boulder Creek crossings
exposed summit block in afternoon thunderstorms
backups.pro_needs: Glacier-travel and crevasse-rescue gear rather than rock protection: a rope, crevasse-rescue hardware, ice axe, and crampons for the glacier chute. No fixed or removable rock protection is typically placed on the Class 3 scrambling sections above the glacier.
backups.approach: Start at the White River Trailhead (~2,300 ft, end of White River Road/FR-6400). Follow White River Trail #1507 south along the flat valley floor for about 4 miles - easy grade but notoriously buggy/mosquito-heavy in early-to-mid summer - to its junction with Boulder Creek Trail #1562. Turn onto Boulder Creek Trail and climb roughly 4.5 miles through forest into Boulder Creek Basin, fording Boulder Creek (unbridged) around 4,000 ft; in early season this crossing is cold and knee-to-thigh deep and sometimes braids into two or three separate channels. Established camps sit in the open basin between about 4,900 and 5,300 ft (roughly 8.5 miles and ~3,000 ft of gain from the car), and given the scale of this outing (~22-23 miles round trip, 6,200-6,500+ ft one-way gain to the summit) most parties treat this as a base camp rather than a car-to-car day. From camp, leave the maintained trail and climb open heather/talus north toward Boulder Pass (~6,300 ft) - a direct fall-line push from about 5,800 ft takes roughly 1.5 hours. Two lines diverge from the pass area: for the glacier line, traverse east across the basin under Peak 7242, crossing its NE ridge near 6,700 ft, then turn west (~30 min) to reach the toe of the Walrus Glacier (marked 'Clark Glacier' on some maps) and rope up for crevassed glacier travel, crampons and axe required. For the non-glacier south-basin alternative, stay climber's-left, gain the south ridge of Pt. 8373 on open heather, and locate what published notes call 'the one and only easy gully' near 7,200-7,300 ft breaching the summit rock band; contour broken rock and lingering snow to the final south/west ridge and a short class 3 scramble to the summit. Water is reliable along the White River and in Boulder Creek Basin but essentially absent above camp - fill up before the push. Key hazards: the unbridged Boulder Creek ford, heavy mosquitoes on the valley approach, wet-slide/avalanche-prone slopes on the basin traverse into early summer, and genuine route-finding difficulty picking the correct gully/ridge above the basin - parties have gotten cliffed out searching for it.
backups.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line back to Boulder Creek Basin camp, then out via Boulder Creek Trail #1562 and White River Trail #1507 to the trailhead. If you climbed via the Walrus Glacier, descend the same glacier line back down to the 6,700 ft bench and over Boulder Pass, staying roped through the crevassed sections and unroping once back on stable moraine/talus below the ice. If you climbed/are descending the non-glacier south-basin alternative, downclimb the same class 3-4 gully and ridge terrain you ascended back to the heather slopes above camp. Watch for lingering wet-snow avalanche debris on the basin traverse below Boulder Pass in early/mid-summer, and re-ford Boulder Creek on the way out. This is fundamentally a long walk-off/scramble descent, not a rappel-dependent one.
backups.bail: This is a non-technical route with no fixed rappel stations, so retreat at any point is simply reversing the ascent line back down the glacier chute to Boulder Pass and out the Boulder Creek Trail. The main complication for a bail is timing the unbridged Boulder Creek ford, which rises later in the day with snowmelt.

pitch_detail.notes: White River Trail to the Boulder Creek Trail junction, about 4 miles, mostly forest.
Climb from Boulder Basin camp northeast to roughly 6,300-ft Boulder Pass, then descend steep snow on the far side to a ~6,700-ft bench on Clark's eastern arm.
Ascend a moderately steep chute on the glacier's left (south) margin, stepping over narrow crevasses and crossing a snow-bridge over one larger crevasse.
Short scramble over the summit rocks above the upper glacier snowfield to the true summit.

itinerary.cal: Boulder Creek fords and lingering snow on the glacier approach are easiest from mid-July through August; the road to White River Trailhead is normally clear by late May but the glacier itself is best climbed before it opens up too much in late summer.

days.note: From the White River Trailhead (2,300 ft), hike the White River Trail about 4 miles, then turn up the Boulder Creek/Boulder Pass Trail, fording Boulder Creek where it braids into several shallow channels. Camp in the basin anywhere from about 4,900 to 5,300 ft with a view of Clark Mountain's south side.

days.objective: Establish base camp in Boulder Basin

days.note: An alpine start from Boulder Basin gains Boulder Pass and the east-ridge bench before dropping onto the Walrus Glacier. Rope up and pick a line up the moderately steep chute on the glacier's left (southern) margin, watching for narrow crevasses, then finish with a Class 3 scramble and a short 45-50 degree snow traverse to the summit block. Reverse the same line back to camp.

schedule.detail: Alpine start with light day packs; rope and glacier gear carried.

schedule.label: Summit block
schedule.detail: Class 3 rock scramble plus a soft 45-50 degree snow traverse to the top.

schedule.label: Back at Boulder Basin camp
schedule.detail: Reverse the glacier and ridge line; full round trip from camp runs roughly 11.5 hours.

days.objective: Climb Clark Mountain (8,602 ft) via the Walrus Glacier and return to camp

days.note: Break camp and retrace the Boulder Creek/Boulder Pass Trail and White River Trail back to the car, re-fording Boulder Creek along the way.
days.title: Hike out

itinerary.totalNote: A 3-day backpack trip: ~7.5 mi/~3,100 ft up to Boulder Basin camp on day 1, an ~8-mile, ~11.5-hour round-trip summit push via the Walrus Glacier on day 2, and the ~7.5-mile hike out on day 3 — roughly 23 miles and 6,500 ft gained/lost total.

access.fees: $5 day-use Northwest Forest Pass or $30 annual Northwest Forest Pass at the White River Trailhead lot
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, available at the White River trailhead kiosk
access.closures: Closed right now: Okanogan-Wenatchee closure order 06-17-07-2026-40 (Little Giant Fire), effective 3 September 2026 through 31 October 2026 unless rescinded sooner, closes FSR 6400 to the end of the road and lists the White River Trailhead, which is this route's access.
access.landManager: Glacier Peak Wilderness, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Wenatchee River Ranger District)
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass required for trailhead parking ($5 day-use ePass or $30 annual)

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk and carry it with you.

road.name: White River Road (Forest Road 6400)
road.driveNote: From Leavenworth, US-2 west ~15 miles to Cole's Corner, then WA-207 (Lake Wenatchee Highway) ~10.5 miles, then White River Road/FS 6400 ~10 miles to the trailhead at road's end; paved/good gravel, generally passable to passenger cars in summer.

climate.typical: Transitional climate between the wetter crest and drier east side; firm mornings.

bySeason.summer: Best window; glacier firm in morning

emergency.notes: Remote wilderness terrain with no cell coverage; carry a satellite communicator. For search and rescue, call 911 for active emergencies or RiverCom dispatch at (509) 663-9911; Chelan County Sheriff's SAR and Chelan County Mountain Rescue are the responding units.
emergency.rangerStation: Wenatchee River Ranger District, 600 Sherbourne St, Leavenworth, WA 98826, (509) 548-2550
emergency.nearestHospital: Cascade Medical Center, Leavenworth, WA — 24-hour ER, roughly 25 road miles from the White River Trailhead via WA-207/US-2

crowds.peakTraffic: Late July-August weekends, especially Mountaineers-affiliated club trips
crowds.estimatePerSeason: unknown exact count - qualitatively 'popular' among Seattle-area alpine scramblers (a known Mountaineers club objective), but the ~23 mile round trip and remote Boulder Pass/Little Giant Pass approach filter out casual traffic; likely well under 50 total parties per season

fitnessSpec.hiking: Very high - roughly 23 miles round trip with on the order of 6,500 ft of cumulative gain; most parties split it into a 2-day overnight rather than a single push
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight backpacking load (shelter, food, glacier travel gear) for the typical 2-day itinerary; day-trippers attempting it in one push carry a lighter but still substantial pack

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long - Boulder Creek Trail over Boulder Pass or Napeequa River Trail over Little Giant Pass, converging near the Napeequa River roughly 3.7 miles east of Boulder Pass, before ascending to the glacier; most parties camp overnight rather than day-tripping
requiredSkills: off-trail routefinding through brush, heather, slabs and morainal debris
basic snow travel with ice axe/crampons
Class 2-3 scrambling comfort, including loose rock near the summit
self-sufficiency for a long, remote wilderness approach with no cell coverage
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate-to-advanced scrambler with prior glacier travel experience; not a beginner objective given the remote approach and Walrus/Clark Glacier crossing

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through September, with August the most reliable month

July.reason: Only the back half of July is typically viable; earlier in the month lingering snow on the approach and less-consolidated glacier bridges are more likely in a transitional season of firm mornings

August.reason: Best window - glacier is firm in the morning and the approach is typically snow-free

September.reason: Still climbable, but crevasses opening more in fall means the reliable window narrows; watch for early-season snowfall late in the month

weather.typical: Transitional climate between the wetter Cascade crest and drier east side, with firm mornings on the glacier
weather.probability: Afternoon convective buildup/thunderstorms are common across the Cascades in August

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Moderate - Class 2-3 scrambling with loose rock near the summit combined with glacier crossing; a fall near crevasses or on the loose summit rock could be serious, though the route lacks sustained high-angle exposure

avalanche.zone: No NWAC forecast zone precisely covers the Chiwawa/Napeequa/Glacier Peak Wilderness area; nearest reference zones are Stevens Pass and East Slopes Central, but NWAC does not issue forecasts during this route's July-September climbing season

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: Real hazard: Walrus Glacier crevasses, opening up further by fall, so rope/crevasse-rescue readiness matters most in September

gaps: No NWAC avalanche zone maps directly onto this remote peak; zone assignment above is an approximation
No quantified per-season party-count data found, only qualitative 'popular Mountaineers objective' language from Mountaineers.org/SummitPost trip reports
Afternoon thunderstorm frequency is inferred from general Cascades summer patterns, not confirmed peak-specific data

Difficulty breakdown (physical/technical/exposure/commitment/routefinding) is a computed starting estimate derived from grade, pitch count, and route data on file -- not a researched or crowd-sourced rating. Users can blend in their own read via the UI.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the White River Trailhead (~2,300 ft) at the end of White River Road / FR-6400 above Lake Wenatchee

backups.rope_type: 30-40m glacier rope (crevasse hazard), unroped for the final rock scramble
backups.rope_note: Route crosses the Walrus (Clark) Glacier before a Class 3 rock finish to the summit. Rope up for glacier travel; standard crevasse-rescue kit (prusiks) recommended. Rock finish from the ~8000' col is typically done unroped.
backups.corrections: None — glacier-crossing requirement confirmed across multiple independent trip reports (Mountaineers, Mazamas, trailcatjim).

approach_variants.name: Boulder Creek and the sheepherder's trail to the south basin — the non-glacier line
approach_variants.notes: Start at the White River trailhead at the end of White River Road, FR 6400, at about 2,300 ft; a Northwest Forest Pass is needed. Walk the White River trail #1507 about four flat miles — one party gained all of three hundred feet in a little over an hour — to the Boulder Creek trail #1562 junction. Turn east up Boulder Creek. At about the 5,000 ft level, roughly four and a half miles up this trail, pick up an old sheepherder's trail heading west and follow it to around 5,600 to 5,700 ft. Note that published mileages on this stretch do not reconcile cleanly between sources, so navigate by elevation and by the basin rather than by a mile count. There is a faint path that contours, crosses the creek and climbs the west side of Boulder Creek, firming up into decent tread as it gains the slope. Leave the sheepherder's trail in the basin above Boulder Creek around 5,700 ft and climb open heather north-north-west to the southern ridge running off Clark's south-east peak, Point 8373. Car to summit is given as about eleven and a half miles one way with roughly 6,500 ft of gain, and essentially every party camps in the Boulder Creek basin rather than trying it in a day.
hazards: Getting cliffed out on the spur while looking for a gully that is really a ledge
Unbridged Boulder Creek crossing, cold and thigh-deep early season and sometimes braided
Losing the sheepherder's trail — it is notoriously hard to find from the White River trail
Heavy mosquitoes on the valley walk
No water above the Boulder Creek basin
approach_variants.baseFinding: Everything turns on one feature and it is misdescribed by its own name. Published descriptions call it the one and only easy gully breaching the ridge — the way down off the spur into Clark's south basin — and it leaves the crest at about 7,200 to 7,300 ft. The correction, from a climber who found it: it is Class 2, and it feels more like a sloping ledge than a gully. Parties hunting for a defined cleft walk past it and get cliffed out. Two accounts both put it at 7,200 ft and both anchor it to the south spur of Point 8373, so the elevation is the reliable half of the identification and the word gully is the unreliable half. The positional cue that puts you in the right place to look: there is a flattish section of the spur at 7,200 ft that is reached easily on scree and grass. Stand on that flat and you can see the south slope of Clark, which looks easy — and it is. The difficulty is purely in getting down to it, which is what the ledge is for. Drop a couple of hundred feet down that ledge, then contour the upper south basin on broken rock and patches of permanent snow to the final south ridge and a short Class 3 scramble to the top. A note on names before you cross-reference anything: the Walrus Glacier is shown as the Clark Glacier on maps. They are one feature with two names.

approach_variants.name: Boulder Pass and the Walrus Glacier — the glacier line
approach_variants.notes:
Approach identically to Boulder Basin: White River trail #1507 four miles to the Boulder Creek trail #1562, then up into the open basin at roughly 5,300 ft, about five to six hours and three thousand feet from the car. That basin is the camp.

From camp, climb north-east to Boulder Pass at about 6,300 to 6,330 ft. Drop down steep snow on the far side, then climb to a bench at about 6,700 ft on Clark's eastern arm.

The bench is where you rope up. Do it there, before you go anywhere, because of what comes next.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Jun-Sep, on the earlier side while the crevasses are still bridged
hazards: Crevasses and snowbridges on the lower Walrus Glacier
Steep snow on the far side of Boulder Pass
No view of the glacier until you have committed around the eastern arm
Unbridged Boulder Creek ford lower down
The 7,200 ft south-basin gully is a landmark for a different route and will mislead you here
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You cannot see the Walrus Glacier until you are committed to it. From the 6,700 ft bench you wrap around Clark's eastern arm, and only then does the glacier come into view for the first time. That is why the bench is the roping-up point rather than the glacier's edge — there is no convenient stopping place once you are round the corner.

The entry is specific and it is not the middle of the toe: go up a moderately steep chute on the left, southern margin of the glacier. Expect to step over several narrow crevasses and, in at least one recorded year, to cross a snowbridge over a large one.

Once on the gentle upper glacier the summit wedge is visible in the distance and the navigation problem is over. The finish skirts the upper south face of that wedge on a steep snowfield and ends with a short scramble onto the summit rocks — about six hours from camp.

Negative marker, and this one matters because it would send you to the wrong landmark entirely: the famous one-and-only-easy-gully at 7,200 ft belongs to the south basin route, not to this one. If you are on the Walrus you never touch it. A published page titled for the Walrus Glacier in fact describes the south-basin line in its turn-by-turn, so read carefully which route a description is actually walking.

climbing_route.label: Boulder Pass to the bench on the eastern arm
climbing_route.notes: From Boulder Basin camp climb north-east to Boulder Pass at about 6,300 ft, go down steep snow on the far side, then climb to a bench at about 6,700 ft on Clark's eastern arm. Rope up on the bench, before moving onto the glacier.

climbing_route.label: Walrus Glacier
climbing_route.notes: Work up the glacier on the east side of the peak by a moderately steep chute along its left (south) margin, stepping over narrow crevasses; at least one bigger crevasse may need a snow bridge. Later in summer the crevasses open further and the line has to zig-zag between them. Above, the upper glacier eases off toward the col below the summit.

climbing_route.label: Summit finish from the col
climbing_route.notes: Unrope at the top of the glacier and cross the upper south side of the summit wedge on steep snow and broken rock, then scramble a short class 2-3 section onto the summit rocks. Following the east ridge from the col is the other way up.

bivy.name: Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin, White River
bivy.notes: This is the standard base for Clark Mountain and the reason Clark is a White River peak rather than a Little Giant one. From the trailhead at about 2,300 feet the White River trail runs flat for four miles, then the Boulder Creek trail turns east and climbs for another seven, crossing Boulder Creek at around 4,000 feet — a wade or a log, and high water there turns parties round early in the season. Good camps exist in a large open basin at about 4,900 feet and again just below the pass around 6,000 feet, with the pass itself at about 6,200 feet holding dry ground even when there is snow about. From the pass the Walrus Glacier route traverses the basin east of the ridge point, crosses the northeast ridge around 6,700 feet and gains the glacier for the east side of the mountain; the whole thing runs to about twenty-five miles round trip and six and a half thousand feet of gain. Tenpeak Mountain is served from the same trailhead by a different drainage — six miles up the White River, then an old unmaintained sheep path toward Thunder Creek and Thunder Basin, with dense slide alder between roughly 4,200 and 5,000 feet that is the hardest part of the day. Tenpeak is a technical summit with a north couloir and a milder-looking southeast face, it sees very few ascents, and most parties want a third day to climb it properly from a basin camp rather than pushing it in one.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and streams through the basin below the pass and at the pass itself well into the season; Thunder Basin runs on creeks that are dependable in summer. The lower Boulder Creek crossing is the water hazard rather than the water supply.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove only up here. The White River road was inside the 2026 fire closure that ran from mid-August to the end of October along with the Chiwawa side, so this approach and the Little Giant one were shut at the same time by the same order — do not assume that losing one leaves the other.
bivy.capacity: Open ground at the pass with plenty of dry spots for several tents, a good basin camp about a mile below it, and separate rough ground over in Thunder Basin for one or two parties
